title: AI Pricing Pressure and Cautious Clients Cloud Indian IT's September Quarter Earnings
excerpt: Five brokerages tell Reuters that India's top IT firms face their weakest sequential quarter in three years as AI-driven price deflation eats into the billable-hours model; guidance cuts loom when TCS reports October 8.
body:
• India's top IT companies are expected to report another weak quarter for July–September, with five brokerages telling Reuters that revenue growth could be the weakest sequential performance in three years and some firms may trim full-year forecasts.
  • Jefferies expects the six largest firms to post quarter-on-quarter revenue growth of just 0.7% to 3.5%; Kotak expects Infosys to cut the top of its 1.5%–3% annual guidance to 2.5%, while Jefferies sees a deeper reset to 0.5%–2%.
  • The culprit is AI-led deflation: automation lets clients complete software work faster and with fewer people, pressuring the billable-hours model that underpins the $315-billion sector — while higher oil prices and interest rates keep client spending cautious.
  • TCS kicks off earnings season on October 8, followed by Infosys, HCLTech, and Wipro later in the month; the Nifty IT index is down about 27% in 2026, lagging the broader market.

India's information technology giants are heading into another soft earnings season. Five brokerages told Reuters that the country's top IT companies are set to report weak results for the September quarter — and could trim their annual revenue growth forecasts — as AI-driven pricing pressure and tepid client spending bite.

According to Reuters, reporting on October 1, the rise of AI-based technology has battered the $315-billion information technology sector, which is especially vulnerable because of its reliance on billable hours. The sector, which employs nearly 6 million people, has been among the market's worst performers over the past year, forcing companies to rejig business models and offer steep discounts.

Context & Background

For years, Indian IT services companies have billed clients based on employee hours and project-based work. AI tools are now automating parts of software development, testing, and infrastructure management — allowing the same work to be done faster, with fewer people. Clients naturally want a share of those savings, and the first negotiation is usually about price.

"AI-led deflation has more legs to go and demand environment is not improving," Jefferies said in a note, citing additional pressure from higher oil prices and interest rates. IT companies typically post strong performance in the first two quarters of the fiscal year on higher billing days and project starts; this year the first quarter was muted, and expectations for the second are similarly subdued.

The numbers tell the story. Jefferies expects the top six firms to grow revenue 0.7% to 3.5% quarter-on-quarter — the weakest sequential performance in three years. Year-on-year, revenue is still expected to rise about 10% in rupee terms, but organic growth after stripping out currency moves looks lackluster. The Nifty IT index has dropped roughly 27% so far in 2026, well behind the benchmark Nifty 50's 13.4% decline.

Impact & Analysis

The stakes go beyond one quarter. Infosys's full-year guidance is the number to watch: Kotak expects the company to trim the top of its 1.5%–3% annual revenue forecast to 2.5%, while Jefferies expects a sharper cut to 0.5%–2%. When a bellwether like Infosys lowers guidance, investors typically assume next year's pipeline is softer too, because corporate tech budgets rarely rebound overnight — often triggering earnings revisions across the sector.

HCLTech and Tech Mahindra are expected to lead the large caps; Wipro is expected to lag, per brokerage forecasts cited by analysts. Acquisitions and deal ramp-ups may flatter some numbers, but underlying organic growth remains weak.

TCS chairman N. Chandrasekaran warned shareholders at the company's June annual general meeting that TCS could eventually have as many AI agents as human employees — "the day is not far when the company will have half a million AI agents." TCS ended FY2026 with 584,519 employees, down from the previous year, even as its annualized AI revenue crossed $2.3 billion and climbed to $2.6 billion by the June quarter. The message is clear: useful technology and profitable monetization are different achievements, and Indian IT is being forced to change the unit in which it gets paid — from hours to outcomes.

Diaspora Angle

The pain is not confined to Bengaluru or Mumbai. India's IT sector is the country's largest private employer of white-collar professionals and a pillar of the diaspora economy — from the engineers who rotate through US client sites on work visas to the NRI investors holding IT stocks and the families back home dependent on tech salaries. A sector repricing itself around AI agents rather than headcount will ripple through campus hiring, on-site postings, and remittance flows alike.

What's Next

TCS reports on October 8, with Infosys, HCLTech, and Wipro following later in the month. Investors will focus on annual revenue forecasts and on how executives describe the AI pricing conversation with clients. Whether guidance cuts are shallow or deep will set the tone for the rest of the October reporting run — and for a sector still searching for its post-AI business model.
image_caption: A data card from analyst Aravind Raghunathan shows the Jefferies forecast of 0.7% to 3.5% quarter-on-quarter revenue growth for India's top six IT firms. The figure would mark the sector's weakest sequential performance in three years as AI-driven pricing pressure and cautious client spending weigh on September-quarter earnings.
nri_angle: India's IT sector anchors diaspora jobs, visa-linked postings, and NRI investment; its forced pivot from billable hours to AI-driven outcomes reshapes prospects for Indian tech professionals at home and abroad.
author: Diaspora Desk
